body.statement: If \(\tau_n=n\rho_n\to\tau\in[0,\infty)\), then the sixty-vector \(K\Rightarrow Z\), and jointly \(n\widehat\Delta^P_{\ell}\Rightarrow T_{\ell}\), \(n\widehat\Delta^E_{\ell}\Rightarrow T_{\ell}\), and \(n\Delta_{\ell}\to\tau(Q_{\ell}-c_{\ell4})\). Hence \(nL^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\widehat\Delta^E_{\ell}\Rightarrow L^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}T_{\ell}\); at \(\tau=0\), this limit equals \(L^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\{\pi_{\ell3}/(2\pi_{\ell1}\pi_{\ell2})-1/(2\pi_{\ell4})\}\), which need not vanish under unequal shares.
body.justification: Bounded expected counts change the experiment itself, so a Gaussian correction cannot describe the sampling law.
body.gap: Marohn supplies general Gaussian--Poisson experiment transitions but not the smoothed nonlinear DiD statistic or its unequal-share zero-intensity limit.
body.consumer: Sparse panels with zero cells obtain a defined non-Gaussian reference law rather than an invalid Wald approximation.
body.proof_tex:
For a fixed cell \((\ell,j)\), Bernoulli role sampling gives the probability generating function
\[
\mathbb E s^{K_{\ell j,n}}
=\{1+r_{\ell j,n}(s-1)\}^{n_{\ell j}}.
\tag{1}
\]
The common-rarity, coefficient-limit, and role-share-limit assumptions imply, when \(n\rho_n\to\tau<\infty\),
\[
n_{\ell j}r_{\ell j,n}\longrightarrow
\pi_{\ell j}\tau c_{\ell j},
\qquad
n_{\ell j}r_{\ell j,n}^2\longrightarrow0.
\tag{2}
\]
Expanding the logarithm in (1) and using (2) gives
\[
\log\mathbb E s^{K_{\ell j,n}}
\longrightarrow \pi_{\ell j}\tau c_{\ell j}(s-1).
\]
Equivalently, direct expansion of the binomial mass function gives convergence at every nonnegative integer to the \(\operatorname{Poisson}(\pi_{\ell j}\tau c_{\ell j})\) mass; (2) also gives tightness by Markov's inequality.  Mutual independence of all role samples and the fixed number \(4L=60\) of cells therefore yield the joint product law
\[
K\Rightarrow Z.
\tag{3}
\]

Set
\[
a_{\ell j,n}=n\widetilde r_{\ell j}
=\frac{n(K_{\ell j,n}+1/2)}{n_{\ell j}+1}.
\]
The role-share limits are strictly positive by the share bounds.  Hence (3), substitution in the preceding explicit formula, and convergence of each deterministic denominator give jointly
\[
a_{\ell j,n}\Rightarrow
W_{\ell j}=\frac{Z_{\ell j}+1/2}{\pi_{\ell j}}.
\tag{4}
\]
Every \(a_{\ell3,n}\) and \(W_{\ell3}\) is strictly positive because of the add-half term.  Consequently ordinary algebra in (4) gives
\[
n\widehat\Delta^P_\ell
=\frac{a_{\ell1,n}a_{\ell2,n}}{a_{\ell3,n}}-a_{\ell4,n}
\Rightarrow
\frac{W_{\ell1}W_{\ell2}}{W_{\ell3}}-W_{\ell4}
=T_\ell.
\tag{5}
\]

It remains to verify that the exact link has the same bounded-count limit.  Fix an integer \(M\).  On
\[
\mathcal F_{n,M}=\{\max_{\ell,j}K_{\ell j,n}\leq M\},
\]
the share bounds place all \(a_{\ell j,n}\), for sufficiently large \(n\), in a compact interval \([d_M,D_M]\subset(0,\infty)\).  The proof of the uniform common-cutoff theorem depends on the coefficient set only through finite positive endpoints; applied with rarity scale \(1/n\) and this interval, it gives, uniformly on \(\mathcal F_{n,M}\),
\[
nH(a_{\ell1,n}/n,a_{\ell2,n}/n,a_{\ell3,n}/n)
=\frac{a_{\ell1,n}a_{\ell2,n}}{a_{\ell3,n}}+O(v_n^{-2}),
\qquad v_n=-q(1/n)\longrightarrow\infty.
\tag{6}
\]
This application is legitimate for large \(n\), since every \(a_{ell j,n}/n\) lies in \((0,1)\), and it uses the exact factorization before applying the uniform remainder.  The limiting product-Poisson vector in (3) is tight; hence
\[
\lim_{M\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}
\Pr(\mathcal F_{n,M}^{c})=0.
\]
First taking \(n\to\infty\) in (6) and then \(M\to\infty\) proves
\[
n\widehat\Delta^E_\ell-n\widehat\Delta^P_\ell\to_P0
\tag{7}
\]
jointly over all pairs.  Equations (5)--(7) prove both statistic limits.

For the population target, the exact factorization and uniform common-cutoff theorem give
\[
H(r_{\ell1},r_{\ell2},r_{\ell3})
=\rho_nQ_{\ell n}+O(\rho_nu_n^{-2}),
\tag{8}
\]
uniformly over pairs; boundedness of \(A_{\ell n}\) and \(Q_{\ell n}\) follows from the coefficient box.  Since \(n\rho_n\to\tau<\infty\), \(u_n\to\infty\), and coefficients converge, the identified causal identity \(\Delta_\ell=H(r_{\ell1},r_{\ell2},r_{\ell3})-r_{\ell4}\) and (8) imply
\[
n\Delta_{\ell n}
=n\rho_n(Q_{\ell n}-c_{\ell4,n})+o(1)
\longrightarrow\tau(Q_\ell-c_{\ell4}).
\tag{9}
\]
Averaging (5)--(7) over the fixed \(L\) pairs gives the claimed aggregate convergence.

If \(\tau=0\), then every Poisson mean is zero, so \(Z_{\ell j}=0\) almost surely and
\[
W_{\ell j}=\frac1{2\pi_{\ell j}},
\qquad
T_\ell
=\frac{\pi_{\ell3}}{2\pi_{\ell1}\pi_{\ell2}}
-\frac1{2\pi_{\ell4}}.
\]
Thus the aggregate limit is exactly the displayed average in the theorem.  Positivity of the shares makes every denominator valid, but no assumption forces the four shares to coincide, so this deterministic limit need not be zero.
